Each firm needs one customized critical input and chooses a home supplier, a foreign supplier, both, or exit. Home is safer and more expensive. There are relationship-specific failures and country-level disruptions. The authors compare firms’ choices with a planner’s choices under differentiated-product competition. With CES preferences, a diversification subsidy achieves the constrained optimum when consumption subsidies are unavailable. With more flexible demand, even the direction of the diversification intervention can change.

title: Supply Chain Resilience: Should Policy Promote International Diversification or Reshoring?
text:
Connection to the other papers
Tomlin asks what one buyer should do; this paper asks whether private choices line up with social welfare. Qualification, reserve capacity and stock policies could determine whether a resilience subsidy actually creates a usable alternative.

title: Supply Chain Resilience: Should Policy Promote International Diversification or Reshoring?
section: A limit to keep in mind
text:
A limit to keep in mind
The source itself proposes dynamics, inventories and richer chains as extensions. Those are starting points for a literature search, not evidence of an unfilled gap. The baseline is very simple: one critical input and two countries. Its public-welfare result is different from the privately optimal sourcing policy of a single buyer.

title: Supply Chain Resilience: Should Policy Promote International Diversification or Reshoring?
text:
Question for the meeting
What exactly would justify a diversification subsidy here? The consulted working paper gives conditional results. Under CES demand and restricted instruments diversification can be the constrained-optimal intervention; broader demand assumptions can change its direction. I would not recommend universal reshoring.

title: Supply Network Formation and Fragility
text:
What I got from this
Having alternatives for one input is useful, but the firm still needs all its essential inputs. In a deep network, a small deterioration across many relationships can therefore matter a lot. I still need to get more comfortable with the threshold argument and how much carries over to a small, finite network.

title: Supply Network Formation and Fragility
text:
How they study it
This is an analytical network/percolation model. Relationship strength is the probability that a link works, and firms invest to improve it. A firm functions only if it has a working supplier for every essential input, whose own inputs must also work. The authors study reliability first with exogenous strengths and then with strategic investment. They identify productive, fragile and unproductive regimes; the fragile regime occurs over a range of parameters, not just at a single accidental parameter value.

title: Supply Network Formation and Fragility
text:
Connection to the other papers
Network Origins has amplification on a given input–output network; this paper adds reliability and strategic relationship investment. Reliability budgets need to consider essential input categories and upstream structure, not just supplier counts.

title: Supply Network Formation and Fragility
section: A limit to keep in mind
text:
A limit to keep in mind
The sharp phase transition depends on the large/deep-network setting. I should not claim that a small finite factory network has a literal discontinuity of the same kind. Multisourcing within an input type and needing multiple input types play different roles. The result is a mechanism, not an estimate of how close today’s economy is to a collapse threshold.

title: Supply Network Formation and Fragility
text:
Question for the meeting
How should I interpret the threshold result for a real, finite network? No. It establishes a threshold mechanism in a large/deep-network model. Applying it requires finite-network data and a check of its essential-input and failure assumptions.

title: The Network Origins of Aggregate Fluctuations
text:
What I got from this
Small shocks do not always average out across the economy. Some sectors supply so many others, directly and indirectly, that their shocks matter much more. This is the basic network idea I need before moving to the newer papers.

title: The Network Origins of Aggregate Fluctuations
text:
How they study it
The authors build a multisector input–output model and study how aggregate volatility changes as the economy is disaggregated. The structure of influence through direct and higher-order supplier connections determines whether the usual diversification argument applies. U.S. input–output data provide an illustrative quantitative exercise, but the paper explicitly says this is not a substitute for a systematic econometric investigation (PDF p. 28).

title: The Network Origins of Aggregate Fluctuations
text:
Connection to the other papers
Baqaee–Farhi adds nonlinear response beyond a first-order approximation; Elliott adds essential-input reliability and endogenous investment. Criticality measures should reflect downstream dependence, although criticality alone does not select an optimal intervention.

title: The Network Origins of Aggregate Fluctuations
section: A limit to keep in mind
text:
A limit to keep in mind
This baseline has a fixed production network. It does not establish how an individual firm should adapt its suppliers during a shock. An economically influential node is not automatically the best intervention target: intervention effectiveness and costs can change the ranking. I should also avoid translating an aggregate asymptotic result directly into a finite supplier portfolio.

title: The Network Origins of Aggregate Fluctuations
text:
Question for the meeting
What do the newer network papers add to this starting point? The propagation foundation is older. The newer questions in this list concern link formation, adaptation, private versus social resilience and richer transaction data. I should describe that progression rather than call the whole field new.
